idee_recherchee.texte: The Big Bang was not an explosion in space but the rapid expansion of space itself from an extremely hot and dense state about 13.8 billion years ago, and the question of what came before it remains unanswered.

titre_video: Scientists Are Freaking Out Over Space Time (It's Not Real)
resume: The Big Bang should have produced equal matter and antimatter that annihilated each other, yet the universe has slightly more matter, about one particle per billion surviving. Scientists cannot explain why, and the divine intervention idea is rejected because it cannot be tested.
texte: Scientists know the universe started with two types of matter. There was regular matter, which is [music] what you and everything else is made of, and then there was antimatter. But today the universe is made almost exclusively of regular matter. Why do we live in a world full of matter instead of a world full of antimatter? This is a great question, and one that scientists don't have an answer for. We think that at the beginning [music] of it all, when the Big Bang created the universe, there was about a 50/50 split between antimatter and matter. When these two forms of matter came into contact, they annihilate, which [music] isn't conducive to constructing the universe we see today. However, for some reason our universe ended up with slightly more matter than antimatter, which is why anything exists at all. If there were even amounts of antimatter and matter, the only thing that would be left in the universe after it all annihilated would be some photons. Obviously, this is not the case. Scientists know that there must have been more matter, but they can't figure out why that would be the case. In fact, it's estimated that only about one matter particle per billion escaped being annihilated just after the Big Bang. This [music] is a really small percentage, but it was enough to create everything we see in the universe today. The craziest part is that the antimatter and the matter mystery is nowhere close to being solved. It just doesn't make sense that mirror copies of particles [music] would not have been produced in the same number during the Big Bang. Perhaps there was some form of divine intervention. The only problem with this theory is that that's not testable, [music] and therefore not an explanation that scientists are willing to accept.
